gaps: The stick-simulation frames border on effect with no subject. The link between the abstract sims and the creature needs to be legible and earned, not just juxtaposed
There is no typographic voice. Titling or credits, if present, should share the stick-system logic
Composition repeats (top-down field after top-down field). It needs camera variety and scale contrast to build a choreographed arc, as D's sequence does
The stick system risks being an effect with no subject. Tie the abstract simulation more tightly to the creature reveal so the idea reads as one arc
The overhead stick frames are flat top-down lighting. Add directional light and depth to match the moody creature shot

Most frames are top-down flat lays of simple extruded primitives. That is close to a 'stock 3D primitive' look, and the rigour of the system has to carry it.

tells: A system-led piece: thousands of rigid-body sticks scattered over saturated grounds in bold, unusual pairings (aubergine on magenta, teal on pink)
The contact-sheet grid of dozens of colour and material variations suggests generative exploration presented as part of the work
A surprise cut to a live or practical creature with a pixel-mosaic face set in mossy natural light. That jump in register adds intrigue
Soft overhead lighting with real contact shadows on the stick fields
Simulation-driven fields of thousands of extruded sticks with physically convincing contact shadows and settling, real rigid-body work rather than a stock primitive placed on its own
Bold, unusual palette pairs (magenta on violet, teal on pink, acid green) varied across a 36-cell grid, showing systematic exploration that reads as a deliberate generative idea
Surprise turn to a photoreal creature in moss, its face a glowing cluster of the same elements, linking the abstract system to an organic subject
No visible typography; the piece leans on pure image, and that partly works, though the grid frame reads a little like a process reel
The palettes are bold and deliberate: magenta against aubergine and teal against pink. The contact-sheet grid shows a systematic colour exploration rather than one default accent.
The physics-driven stick and shard simulations imply real choreography (scatter, pile, reform), and the grid frame suggests a montage of rhythm-cut variations.
There is a surprising turn: the abstract sticks resolve into a photoreal, feathered, bird-like creature with a pixel-shard face in a lush mossy setting. That surprise is evidence of a concept.
There is no visible type. Its absence suits a music-led abstract piece but adds nothing.
Full CG character film with strong character design: a weathered old man with sculpted skin, cloth and beard detail, and a robot with designed wear and panel logic
Motivated practical light: candle-lit interior, firelight rim on clasped hands, volumetric haze in the industrial set
Cinematic language: anamorphic letterbox, a cut from medium shot to insert close-up, a hero pose against an atmospheric depth plate
The key-art frame (teal/magenta, lens flare, sci-fi wordmark) is a genre-standard poster rather than a typographic idea
gaps: The idea is genre boilerplate (grizzled hunter vs. killer robot). It needs a premise or visual conceit that only this film could have, the way D's handmade-evidence conceit does
The palette moves between stock teal/magenta key art and warm orange/teal interiors. Commit to one authored, unusual palette
The typography is a generic sci-fi display wordmark set on the poster. Make the type part of the film's world, distressed and integrated as in D

No type apart from the platform watermark. Its absence suits a performance-led music video
gaps: The setting (dancer alone in an empty warehouse) is a familiar music-video default. A less expected space would raise originality
The palette is safe and muted. A more authored colour decision would make every frame a poster, as D's monochrome does
Neither the frames nor any title treatment carry graphic design or type intent. Nothing extends the lattice idea into the film's identity

tells: The landmark Se7en title sequence: the idea is the killer's obsessive notebooks, so the film's psychology is told through handmade evidence
Typography with a point of view: hand-scratched, jittering, multi-exposed type, with the 7 standing in for the V in the wordmark
Dense, layered frames: taped photos, hooks, cramped handwriting, razor work on fingertip prints
Grim near-monochrome palette with selective sepia and a red accent; macro texture and raking light on paper and skin
Implied motion: rapid cutting, double exposure, focus racks and frame jitter create dread
gaps: Against the year's best it is hard to fault. The only gap is that its influence has made this grimy-collage look a cliché, which says more about later imitators than about this piece
Some frames run very dark and murky. The occasional hero frame could take more legible contrast
This is the benchmark; any remaining gap is marginal

tells: Fully rigged, groomed and shaded characters (bearded hunter, knitted cap, worn leather jacket), well beyond template or AI level
Firelight and candlelight interiors with motivated warm key light, volumetric haze and real material response
Cinemascope framing and a cut-in on hands at the fire show an editorial plan from wide shot to insert

Reads as a studio open-movie and technology showcase, not a work with an authored motion-design voice

gaps: Frames are beautiful but sit within a known music-video vocabulary (dancer in an empty warehouse). Push the setting as far as the VFX idea
The palette is tasteful but safe. C's monochrome-plus-red is more ownable

tells: The type has a clear point of view: hand-scratched, distressed letterforms with the '7' replacing the 'V' in SE7EN. The type tells the story instead of just labelling it.
The textures are physical and obsessive: notebook pages packed with handwriting, tape, hooks, contact sheets and graph paper, layered into dense collage frames.
The lighting is motivated and moody: a hard raking shaft across the hands on the drafting surface, and an extreme macro on graphite or film grain.
The palette is restrained to sepia, black and dirty white with one red accent (the razor or pen line). That restraint reads as deliberate and fits the subject.
The four frames vary widely (macro, collage, type card, insert shot) but share one grammar, which suggests careful edit choreography and stuttering, scratched-film motion.
The idea belongs only to this piece: the killer's process, shown as the title sequence itself.
gaps: This is the benchmark entry. Its only gap is colour, where the near-monochrome limits range and the piece relies on one red accent.
Some insert frames (the graphite macro) read as abstract texture, so they depend on the edit for meaning.
The letterboxed framing is inconsistent across frames, with mixed crops.

tells: The idea is specific and memorable: a dancer's body progressively replaced by a tracked 3D Voronoi lattice. The VFX is the subject, not decoration.
The body tracking and integration hold up in close-up (the shirt lifted to reveal the lattice), which is high-end compositing.
The location is real, with naturalistic window light and a worn warehouse texture. The palette is a considered desaturated teal-grey with yellow pillars and the pink garment as the only warm accent.
The frames progress clearly, from a reveal to a close portrait to a mid-motion turn to a full-body lattice in a wide shot. That progression implies narrative choreography.
There is no type beyond the broadcaster bug. Its absence serves the piece, since this is a performance-led film where type would intrude.
gaps: There is no graphic or typographic layer. Compared with A, the design authorship sits wholly in VFX and cinematography.
The compositions are conventionally centred music-video framing, with less poster-like graphic tension than A.
The palette and location (the grungy empty warehouse) are a familiar music-video trope. The idea carries the originality while the setting does not.

tells: The rendering is competent and production-grade: candle- and fire-lit interiors with volumetric haze and detailed character and robot assets. This is studio-level work (an open-movie production), not AI or template output.
The key-art frame is genre-generic: an angry old warrior, a pink-lit robot, a lone silhouette before a megastructure, and teal-magenta neon. These are well-worn sci-fi poster tropes.
The type is a stock 'techy' sci-fi display face beside a software logo, set as a marketing lockup with no integration into the image.
The cinematic frames rely on letterboxed, underexposed orange-and-black grading. The moodiness is competent but the palette is the default action-short look.
gaps: Find a specific idea beyond 'grizzled hero vs robot'. A builds its whole piece from one obsessive, subject-specific concept.
Give the typography a point of view. Replace the generic sci-fi display face with letterforms that carry the story, as A's scratched SE7EN does.
Push the palette and the frames beyond genre convention (teal/magenta key art, orange firelight) toward a distinctive graphic world where every frame works as a poster.
